background.definition: Chronic prostatitis is a syndrome of genital or pelvic pain that lasts more than 3 months in adult men. Chronic prostatitis is now called chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS) to separate it from acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis (see ). CPPS is further classified into inflammatory and noninflammatory subtypes based on the presence or absence of leucocytes in expressed prostatic secretions, postprostate massage urine, or semen.

list.listitem: 3.3/1000 men per year for CPPS.
The overall lifetime prevalence of chronic prostatitis is approximately 10% to 14%.
Only 2% to 5% of chronic prostatitis cases are chronic bacterial prostatitis; the remainder are cases of CPPS.
The prevalence is higher in men younger than 50 years.
The annual cost per person affected is $4400.
Approximately $84 million is spent in treating patients with chronic prostatitis, excluding indirect costs like loss of work and productivity.
CPPS accounts for 1% of primarycare visits and 8% of urological visits in the US. CPPS accounts for 2 million outpatient visits per year.
It is the most common cause for a visit to a urologist in men younger than 50 years.

National Insitute of Health classify the prostatitis syndrome into 4 catogaries (acute bacterial prostatitis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome [CP/CPPS] and asymptomatic prostatitis). CP/CPPS (CPPS) is a common urologic disorder for men under 50.

The UPOINT system was developed to effectively treat CP/CPPS. The clinical symptoms are catogorized into 6 compnents (urinary symptoms, psychological dysfunction, organ-specific symptoms, infectious causes, neurologic dysfunction, pelvic floor muscle tenderness).

The cause or causes of CPPS are unknown. It is thought to be due to a complex mechanism involving the impaired functions of immunologic, endocrine, neurologic, and psychological factors. Viruses, yeasts, and bacteria causing sexually transmitted disease have been suggested as possible causes.
Common microorganisms associated with chronic bacterial prostatitis include E. coli (80%), Proteus mirabilis, enterococci, and Pseudomonas.
The pathophysiology underlying this syndrome is unknown but may result from several distinct causes (see Causes).
Patients with chronic prostatitis/CPPS typically present with frequency, dysuria, and perineal pain. C
Urinalysis and urine culture are recommended for all patients with suspected chronic prostatitis. C
The 2-glass (or 4-glass) test is the diagnostic test of choice for patients with suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Rectal examination shows enlarged prostate/abnormal imaging study/hematuria

list.listitem: Determine the impact of symptoms on quality of life, which may aid in determining treatment. Also, ask whether the patient has a history of urethritis or sexually transmitted disease to rule out these causes.
Recurrent episodes of UTI, perineal discomfort, and sexual dysfunction with no symptoms between attacks suggest chronic bacterial prostatitis.

Patients may report symptoms for months or years with penile or pelvic pain involving testis, suprapubic, inguinal, and sacral regions. They may also report urinary symptoms (such as hesitancy, urgency, and a sense of incomplete evacuation of the bladder) and sexual symptoms (such as painful ejaculation and hematospermia). These symptoms suggest CPPS.
Pain has more impact on QoL than urinary symptoms.

Severity of the pain and location of the pain vary between patients. Perineal pain/discomfort is common (63%). Other symptoms include testicular pain (58%), pubic area pain (42%) penile pain (32%) with ejaculation pain (45%) or voiding difficulties (43%).
Perform a complete abdominal examination, including examination of hernial orifices. Examine external genitalia for testicular masses and examine the perianal area.

Perform a digital rectal examination. The size and consistency of the prostate is typically normal in men with CPPS and chronic bacterial prostatitis. If the prostate is hard or irregular, consider prostate cancer. If tender, consider acute bacterial prostatitis and, less commonly, chronic bacterial prostatitis. High anal sphincter tone suggests spastic neuropathy of pelvic musculature, while pelvic wall tenderness suggests tension myalgia.
Further evaluation is planned according to history and physical examination findings (see Diagnostic testing).
Obtain a urinalysis and culture from a midstream urine sample, and perform the 2-glass (or 4-glass) test. The 2-glass test (premassage and postmassage only) is nearly as accurate and more convenient.

Evaluation of patients with CPPS should include the following as clinically indicated: Lower urinary tract localization test. Symptom inventory using The National Institute of Health Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index (NIH-CPSI) Questionnaire (13-item index developed to assess symptoms and quality of life in men with Chronic Prostatitis/Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome. Flow rate and residual urine determination. Urine cytology/cystoscopy should be performed in all patients with chronic prostatitis who have microscopic hematuria. Semen analysis and culture should be considered in infertile patients with CPPS. Urethral swab for nucleic acid amplificaton test should be done in patients with symptoms of urethritis and high-risk sexual behavior and chlamydial or gonococcal infections are a consideration. Pressure flow studies and video urodynamics provide information about functioning of the lower urinary tract. Transrectal ultrasound helps to identify other causes of chronic pelvic pain, such as seminal vesicle or ejaculatory abnormalities. Consider pelvic imaging (ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI) to identify anatomic abnormalities of the lower urinary tract. Order prostate-specific antigen in patients older than 50 years or with an irregular, hard, or nodular prostate. These patients should also have a biopsy.
Chronic prostatitis/CPPS is a diagnosis of exclusion.
All patients with chronic prostate symptoms should have a urinalysis, urine culture, and the 2-glass or 4-glass test.

Consider the following additional tests: prostate-specific antigen (if there is an abnormal digital rectal examination result, patient is older than 50 years, or has a family history or risk of prostate cancer), urethral swab (if patient has high-risk sexual behaviors, dysuria, penile pain, or urethral discharge), semen culture (if semen is discolored or foul), urodynamic studies (if there is a change in urine flow, residual urine), cystoscopy (if there is hematuria or abnormal cytology), and transrectal ultrasound/CT/MRI (if other test results are abnormal).
Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin) for 4 weeks are effective for chronic bacterial prostatitis. A
A recent Cochrane systematic review and meta analysis concludes alpha blockers may reduce the prostatic symptoms with minor increase in adverse events.

Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin) for 4 weeks are equally effective and reduce symptoms as well as providing bacteriologic cure. Rates of clinical success at 6 months, defined as the resolution or improvement of symptoms, were between 75% and 89%, and the rates of bacteriologic cure were between 60% and 80%. The best current evidence indicates that antibiotics modestly reduce symptom scores.
A meta-analysis showed treatments including alpha-blockers, antibiotics, and a combination of the two, for CPPS are mostly ineffective. There is a substantial placebo effect with treatment.
The best current evidence indicates that antibiotics only modestly reduce symptom scores in CPPS.

Treatment with alpha-blockers (alfuzosin, terazosin, doxazosin, and tamsulosin) for 3 to 6 months caused a small reduction in symptoms in some small studies, especially when used in patients with a new diagnosis and in treatment-naive patients. However, the best study to date which randomized 272 men to alfuzosin or placebo for 12 weeks found no benefit. Overall, evidence is weak on the benefit of alpha-blockers. A meta-analysis of small studies indicates that a small, and probably not clinically meaningful, improvement results from the use of alpha-blockers. This same meta-analysis indicates a number needed to treat of 8 for a "treatment response" to alpha-blockers.
The combination of antibiotics and alpha blockers may benefit some patients.

5- ARI (Finasteride) reduces symptoms, especially in patients with coexisting benign prostatic hyperplasia. In a select subgroup of patients with CPPS in a prostate cancer risk-reduction study, patients taking dutasteride had improvement in prostate symptoms (NNT = 8). These 5-alpha reductase inhibitors may be an option in select patients.

Anti inflamatory agents (corticosteroids, NSAIDs and thiocolchicoside) may improve prostatitis symptoms without major side effects. Other agents used to improve symptoms include phtotherapy, intraprostatic BTA (botulinum toxin A) injection, Traditional Chinese Medicine are used with varying sucess. Other agents used in various trials include Anticholinergics, Antidepressants, Mepartricin, OM-89 (Escherichia coli lysate), Pentosan, Phosphodiesterase inhibitors, Tanezumab.
Evidence is lacking for allopurinol to treat CPPS.

Despite the potential role of neuropathic pain as a cause of CPPS, pregabalin does not demonstrate clinically significant symptom improvement. A Cochrane review found one RCT that shows that pregabalin does not help patients with CPPS.

Recent coochrane review on CPPS found Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (where shock waves are passed through the skin to the prostate), and Trans rectal thermotherapy (which applies heat to the prostate and pelvic muscle area) compared to medical therapy alone or with medical therapy is beneficial in reliving symptoms.
Multi modal treatment may be more effective than single form of therapy.

An RCT of 89 men with CPPS randomized them to 10 weeks of real or sham acupuncture twice weekly. A clinically important decrease in symptom scores was more common in those receiving acupuncture (73% vs 47%, NNT = 4) and persisted after discontinuation (NNT = 5). A systematic review concluded their may be a role for accupuncture in CPPS.
20 accupunture sessions over 2 months clinically improves symptoms compared to sham accupuncture for chronic pelvic pain related to chronic prostatitis.
Saw palmetto is not effective in CPPS.
Phytotherapy (particularly quercetin and cernilton)is benificial with minimal side effects.
Biofeedback-based pelvic floor training reduces symptoms in CPPS.
Recurrence is common in chronic bacterial prostatitis. C
Most patients with new-onset CPPS report improvement at 6 months. B
The natural history of chronic bacterial prostatitis has not been well studied.
There is only a slight improvement in symptom scores for patients with CPPS over a 2-year interval. However, one third of patients report moderate to marked improvement in overall symptoms.
Recurrence of infection is common following chronic bacterial prostatitis and occurs in one third of patients.

Most patients (66%) with new-onset CPPS report improvement in 6 months (defined as the absence of symptoms in the preceding month). Patients with previous episodes and more severe symptoms are at a higher risk for chronic pelvic pain. The mean improvement of symptom scores was 5 points (of a total 43 points) after 2 years on the National Institutes of Health Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index (NIH-CPSI).
Depression symptoms and pain intensity predict poor quality of life in patients with CPPS.

Chronic bacterial prostatitis: Patients should be monitored for symptoms, and urine culture should be repeated if symptoms recur. As recurrence occurs in one third of patients, urine culture after 6 months is useful.

feature.caption: Classification of Prostatitis.
feature.feature_body:
Number Category Characteristic Features
I Acute bacterial prostatitis Acute bacterial infection of the prostate with symptoms suggestive of UTI. Bacteriuria and pyuria are present
II Chronic bacterial prostatitis Recurrent infection usually caused by same organism
III Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome Chronic pelvic pain and symptoms on voiding and ejaculation without urinary tract infection
IIIA Inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome Leukocytes in the expressed prostatic secretions, postprostate massage urine, or semen
IIIB Noninflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome No leukocytes in the expressed prostatic secretions, postprostate massage urine, or semen
IV Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis Absence of any urinary symptoms detected incidentally during evaluation for other disorders by presence of leukocytes in expressed prostatic secretions or semen
From Krieger JN, Nyberg L, Jr., Nickel JC. NIH consensus definition and classification of prostatitis. JAMA 1999;282:236-237.
